source.title: Can We Remove the Square-Root in Adaptive Gradient Methods? A Second-Order Perspective
source.authors: Wu Lin; Felix Dangel; Runa Eschenhagen; Juhan Bae; Richard E. Turner; Alireza Makhzani

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper, including appendices and experimental tables.
record.tranche_reason: It compares adaptive optimizers with SGD on held-out image-classification performance, using a different optimizer intervention and modern tuning recipe from the cited optimizer comparisons.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-error comparisons for several optimizers and models. Figure 2 also reports a figure-only comparison under an older training setup; the tables provide numerical results for the modern setup.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares held-out error under adaptive optimizers and SGD, and tests whether changing adaptive updates removes the difference. It bears on V4, but its modern experiments tune momentum, weight decay, damping and moment coefficients as well as learning rates; they do not reproduce V4's limited-tuning condition.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' main empirical conclusion: their root-free adaptive recipes close the CNN test-performance gap to SGD while maintaining root-based performance on vision attention models. The intervention also changes initialization and loss scaling, so this is not evidence that deleting the square root alone suffices under an unchanged recipe.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares AdamW, RMSProp variants, Shampoo variants, and SGD using modern learning-rate schedules and two-stage random search; it also removes the square root from adaptive methods. It is not a direct replication of the original optimizer comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported optimizer ranking varies by architecture and dataset: AdamW has higher test error than SGD on the three CIFAR100 CNNs, while the ImageWoof10 models show lower errors for AdamW and other adaptive methods. Figure 2 reports a different outcome with a constant learning rate, default zero preconditioner initialization, and default scaling of an averaged mini-batch loss.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; PMLR 235, 2024
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the tabulated test errors. The paper reports best runs from a two-stage random search, so the tables do not show variability across the 100-run stages. Several additional comparisons appear only as plots.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1, Figure 2, Figures 3, 9, and 10, and Figure 11 contain additional optimizer comparisons or fine-tuning results, but are not included as rows because the tables provide separate numerical results for the primary tested architecture groups; the plots do not provide exact textual values. Figure 2's qualitative older-setup outcome is noted in method_sensitivity.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy under matched architectures and recipes.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.

A controlled comparison of learning-rate/schedule-only tuning against broader tuning; switching Adam to SGD; isolating decoupled weight decay; and whether worse held-out performance occurs despite equal or better training performance. Language evidence includes a plotted LSTM experiment, but the supplied text does not establish its final optimizer ranking numerically.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples.

missing.what: ResNet50/CIFAR100 test-error comparisons of SGD, RMSProp and RF-RMSProp under cross-entropy and square-error losses. These additional architecture/loss conditions are neither recorded nor declared in rows_left_out; optimizer rankings require readable curves.

record.verdict_notes: All tabulated values and SGD baselines match the supplied text. Tables report the best selected run after two 100-run search stages, with results averaged over the last 10 iterations; these are not averages across independent runs, and no uncertainty is supplied. The declared plot omissions do not independently require missing entries. Reversed row states describe optimizer ranking; they do not contradict V4's explicit allowance for broader-tuning reversals.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Language benchmarks; broader tuning beyond the paper's two-stage random search; switching from Adam to SGD; decoupled weight decay as a causal intervention.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.

relationships.condition: AdamW versus SGD on ResNet34, DenseNet121 and VGG16 on CIFAR100, with broad hyperparameter search and step decay
relationships.reason: R21, R24 and R27 show AdamW errors of 24.85, 23.30 and 27.42 versus SGD's 20.91, 19.88 and 24.02; the adaptive disadvantage persists here even with broader tuning.
relationships.display_finding: AdamW has higher test errors than SGD across all three architectures despite broader tuning, with no reported uncertainty for these comparisons.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: AdamW versus SGD on ResNet34, DenseNet121 and VGG16 on CIFAR100, with broad hyperparameter search and step decay
source_check.reason: R21/R22, R24/R25 and R27/R28 show higher AdamW error: 24.85 versus 20.91, 23.30 versus 19.88, and 27.42 versus 24.02. These support the adaptive-disadvantage ordering even under this broader search, without testing the limited-tuning condition itself.

relationships.condition: AdamW and other adaptive methods on GCViT, SwinViT, FocalNet and VMamba on ImageWoof10, with broad tuning and cosine schedules
relationships.reason: R1–R20 show every reported adaptive optimizer below its corresponding SGD test error; this establishes an architecture-and-recipe boundary, consistent with V4 allowing reversals beyond limited tuning.
relationships.display_finding: Verified adaptive comparisons had lower test errors than SGD across the architectures, while some VMamba results remain unverified and uncertainty was unreported.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: AdamW and other adaptive methods on GCViT, SwinViT, FocalNet and VMamba on ImageWoof10, with broad tuning and cosine schedules
source_check.reason: R1–R20 show adaptive-favorable ordering under broad tuning, a possibility V4 already explicitly allows. This condition does not require a new qualification of V4 and does not establish that expanding the tuning search caused the ordering.

relationships.condition: RF-RMSProp on ResNet34 on CIFAR100 with broad tuning and step decay
relationships.reason: R23 leaves only a 0.34-point disadvantage versus SGD, much smaller than AdamW's 3.94-point disadvantage in R21.
relationships.display_finding: RF-RMSProp reportedly had a much smaller deficit than AdamW, but the RF-RMSProp comparison remains unverified.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: RF-RMSProp on ResNet34 on CIFAR100 with broad tuning and step decay
source_check.reason: Table 2 gives RF-RMSProp 21.25 versus SGD 20.91, compared with AdamW 24.85 in R21/R22. This substantially smaller deficit identifies an optimizer-specific qualification; the intervention changes the adaptive update, initialization and scaling.

relationships.condition: RF-RMSProp on DenseNet121 and VGG16 on CIFAR100 with broad tuning and step decay
relationships.reason: R26 and R29 essentially match SGD at 19.81 versus 19.88 and 24.00 versus 24.02, showing that these adaptive updates avoid the disadvantage.
relationships.display_finding: RF-RMSProp nearly matched SGD: its errors were 19.81 and 24.00, compared with SGD's 19.88 and 24.02, respectively. Uncertainty was not reported.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: RF-RMSProp on DenseNet121 and VGG16 on CIFAR100 with broad tuning and step decay
source_check.reason: R25/R26 and R28/R29 give near-equality: 19.81 versus 19.88 and 24.00 versus 24.02, consistent with the authors' gap-closure interpretation. The root-free update provides an optimizer-specific qualification to the deficits of ordinary AdamW under the same broad-search setup.

relation.reason: Reports its own optimizer comparisons measuring the held-out performance ordering named by V4.

tranche.reason: Directly tests adaptive-versus-SGD held-out performance using different adaptive updates and modern training and tuning protocols.

source_check.notes: Tables 1 and 2 average the last 10 iterations, not independent training seeds; no uncertainty is reported for these cells. The root-free recipe changes preconditioner initialization and minibatch scaling as well as removing the root.

statements.correction: Table 1: ImageWoof10 GCViT test error, AdamW 13.48, SGD 14.74; 300 epochs; cosine schedule; two-stage search with 100 runs per stage. Adaptive-favorable ordering under broad tuning; no controlled narrow-to-broad tuning comparison; no challenge to V4's stated limited-tuning condition.
statements.problem: The GCViT numbers and broad-tuning description are correct, but the challenges label conflicts with V4's explicit allowance for adaptive advantages beyond limited tuning.
